transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, um... it's a lot of things, really. I've just been feeling so incredibly heavy lately, you know? Like this thick fog just rolled in and settled right over my life, and I can't seem to shake it. But... well, the thing that actually scared me enough to make an appointment—and I really hesitated to come in, I did, because it sounds so crazy—is what's been happening at work. 

I work surveillance, you see. I'm a surveillance officer at a casino, which means I spend long, long hours in this dark, quiet room just staring at banks of monitors. It's usually very routine, very quiet, especially during the graveyard shift. But lately, during those really quiet stretches, when it's just me and the screens... I've been hearing things. Through the monitor speakers. I'll be sitting there, and suddenly I'll hear these voices, clear as day, saying things to me. They say, "You missed it, Ruth," or... or they'll say, "People are going to get hurt because of you." 

And the terrifying part—the part that really made me realize something is terribly wrong—is that I check the equipment. I check it every time. I'll look down and every single channel is muted. The volume is completely off. And I've even asked the other guards when they come in to relieve me, or if someone pops their head in, if they heard anything over the comms, and they look at me like I'm crazy. No one else hears it. Just me. Sitting there in the dark, with the volume off, hearing these awful, awful things telling me I'm failing and people are going to suffer because I'm not doing my job right. It's just... it's really starting to wear me down, doctor. I don't know what's real anymore when I'm in that room.
Do the voices you hear ever tell you to do something specific?

No... no, they don't give me commands, if that's what you mean. They don't tell me to, you know, go do something or... or act a certain way. It's more like they're just... commenting on me. Judging me. Like I said, it's always things like, "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." It's never "Go do this" or "Go hurt that person." It's just this constant, heavy criticism. 

And I mean, it's bad enough just hearing that, right? Because when you're sitting in that room, and the monitors are glowing, and the air conditioning is humming that low, steady hum... your mind already plays tricks on you. You're looking for cheats, you're looking for sleight of hand, you're looking for a dealer who might be pocketing chips. You have to be so hyper-vigilant. So to have these voices—these completely disembodied voices—telling you that you're failing, that you're missing the very things you're paid to catch... it just paralyzes you. 

I'll sit there and I'll replay the tape in my head, thinking, did I miss a hand at table four? Was that guy at the roulette wheel acting suspicious? And the voices just keep confirming my worst fears, just... feeding into this awful, sinking feeling I have all the time now. But no, they never tell me to actually *do* anything. They just want me to know how terrible I am at my job, and how I'm going to be responsible for something awful happening. It's exhausting, doctor. It really is.
Do you ever hear these voices when you're not at work or in front of the monitors?

Well, that's... that's the thing that really pushed me over the edge to make this appointment, actually. It's... it's just at work. Or, well, mostly at work, in that specific room. I mean, I'll be at home, and I'll feel that heavy, awful fog I was telling you about, just this crushing weight where I can barely get off the couch to make a cup of tea, but the house is quiet. It's just... sad quiet, you know? 

But at work... that's where it happens. Like I was saying before, it's during those quiet stretches in the surveillance room. I'll be sitting there, staring at the screens—table four, the high-roller baccarat, the slot banks near the main entrance—and then I'll hear them. Through the monitor speakers. It's always those same kinds of things, too. "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." And it's so clear, doctor. It's not a mumble, it's not static that my brain is turning into words. It sounds like someone is keyed into the mic, speaking directly to me. 

And I know I already mentioned this, but it's the part that just makes my blood run cold... I check the board. I look down at the console, and every single channel is muted. The little red lights are on, showing the volume is completely off. And I'm just sitting there, frozen, listening to these voices tell me I'm failing, when the equipment is literally turned off. And no one else hears it! If Steve or Marcus walks in to hand off paperwork, they don't hear a thing. It's just me, in that room, hearing these awful things through dead speakers. So, no, I don't hear them at the grocery store or in my living room, thank God, but... but knowing they're waiting for me in that surveillance room, it makes going to work feel like walking to my own execution.
Do you ever hear the voices through anything other than the monitor speakers at work?

Well, um... no, it's just... it's just the monitor speakers. I mean, I know I've been talking a lot about those speakers, but it's because that's exactly what scared me enough to finally come in and see you. It's so specific, you know? It's not coming from the air vents, or... or the hum of the fluorescent lights, or my own head. It's always, always during those long, quiet stretches in the surveillance room. 

I'll be sitting there, and the room is just dead silent, except for maybe the faint sound of the AC, and then... there they are. Coming right through those little black speakers mounted under the screens. And they say the exact same awful things—"You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." 

And I just... I can't stress this enough, doctor, because this is the part that makes me feel like I'm completely losing my mind... I check the board. I look right at the console, and every single channel is muted. The little red lights are glowing, telling me the volume is completely off. The equipment is basically dead to the room. And yet, there are the voices, coming through those dead speakers. 

And like I said, no one else hears a thing. If Marcus comes in to drop off a logbook, I'll ask him, "Did you hear that?" And he just looks at me like I've got two heads. He doesn't hear anything. It's just me, hearing these terrible, critical voices through muted monitor speakers. So no, it's not the radio in my car, it's not the TV at home... it's just those speakers in that room, telling me I'm a failure when the sound is completely turned off.
Do you ever see things that aren't there?

No... no, I don't see anything. It's just the hearing. Just the voices. And I know I keep coming back to this, and I'm sorry to keep repeating myself, but it's just... it's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. Because the seeing part, my vision, that's fine. I stare at those screens for eight, ten hours a shift, looking for the tiny things—a chip slid off the table, a dealer palming a card, someone signaling across the floor. My eyes are sharp. I don't see monsters, I don't see shadows moving, I don't see people who aren't there. 

But what scared me so badly, what finally made me pick up the phone and call this office, is what I'm *hearing*. Because like I was saying, it's those quiet stretches in the surveillance room. The room is dim, the monitors are glowing, and then... there they are. Through those little black monitor speakers. "You missed it, Ruth." "People are going to get hurt because of you." 

And I just... I can't get over the fact that the board is muted. I look down, and the little red lights are on, showing every single channel is completely turned off. The equipment is dead. But the voices are there, clear as day, telling me I'm a failure. And Marcus or Steve will walk in, and they don't hear a single thing. Not a whisper. Just me, hearing these awful things through dead speakers. So no, I don't see things, doctor. My eyes are doing exactly what they're supposed to do. It's my ears... or my mind, I guess... that's the problem.
How do you feel or what do you do immediately after hearing these voices through the monitor speakers?

Well, um... it's... it's just this overwhelming sense of dread, honestly. I mean, the second I hear them—when that voice says, "You missed it, Ruth"—my heart just drops right into my stomach. It's like... it's like ice water in my veins. 

Because, you see, I'm sitting there in that dim room, and the air conditioning is humming, and I'm staring at these glowing screens, and suddenly it's like the walls are closing in on me. I immediately look down at the console, like I've told you, to check the red lights. I just stare at them, those little red mute lights, and I think, "This can't be happening. The sound is off." And I'll reach out, my hand will actually be shaking, and I'll tap the mute button on and off, on and off, just to make sure the board isn't glitching. But it never is. 

And then... then that heavy, awful fog I was telling you about, the one that keeps me on the couch at home? It just rolls right into the surveillance room. It settles over me like a wet wool blanket. I feel so incredibly useless, so incompetent. Because the voices are telling me I'm failing, that people are going to get hurt, and I start to believe them. I start second-guessing everything I'm seeing on the screens. Did I miss a chip? Did I miss a hand signal? 

Sometimes I'll even rewind the footage. I'll pull up the digital playback for table four or the slot banks, and I'll watch the last ten minutes over and over again, squinting at the screen, trying to find whatever it is they're telling me I missed. But there's never anything there. Everything is normal. But I still feel this crushing guilt, this absolute certainty that I'm terrible at my job and that something awful is going to happen because of me. 

And if Marcus walks in right then, while I'm spiraling, I just freeze. I pretend I'm intensely focused on the monitors, hoping he doesn't notice that I'm sweating or that I look like I'm about to cry. I just sit there, trapped in that room, waiting for the shift to end so I can go home and sink back into the couch. It's just... it's exhausting, doctor. It completely drains the life out of me.
Are the voices always critical of your performance at work, or do they ever say anything positive?

Positive? Oh, no... no, never. I wish they did. I really do, but no, they never say anything good. Not a single encouraging word. I know I keep repeating myself, doctor, and I really am sorry, I know I've told you this like three times already today, but it's just... I can't let it go because it's the exact reason I got so terrified that I finally came in to see you. Because it's always, always those same awful, critical things. 

Like I was saying, it happens during those long, quiet stretches in the surveillance room. I'll be sitting there, and the voices will start coming through the monitor speakers, and they never say, "Good catch, Ruth," or "You're doing a great job today." It's only ever, "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." 

And I'll sit there staring at the console, looking at the little red lights showing that every single channel is completely muted, just praying the voices will stop or at least say something nice for a change, just to give me a break. But they don't. They just keep tearing me down, telling me I'm making these horrible mistakes and that I'm responsible for terrible things happening, even though the equipment is completely dead and no one else in the room hears a thing. If Marcus or Steve are there, it's just silence to them. But for me, it's just this constant, heavy criticism coming through those dead speakers, telling me I'm a total failure. So, no... nothing positive. Just the bad.
Do you feel anything else immediately after hearing these voices, besides the overwhelming sense of dread?

Well, yes, besides the dread, it's... it's this incredibly heavy, crushing feeling of guilt. And just... just utter worthlessness. I mean, the dread hits first, like I said, that ice water in my veins, but right on its heels is this absolute conviction that they're right. That the voices are telling the truth. 

I'll be sitting there in the dark, the AC humming, and I just start spiraling. I keep replaying every single thing I've done on shift. Every missed camera angle from three weeks ago, every time I was a second too late calling down to the floor about a suspicious player... I just replay it all over and over in my head like it's a highlight reel of my failures. It feels like absolute proof that I am just completely careless. That I'm actually dangerous to the people working down there. 

And it's so strange, doctor, because logically I know the board is muted, I know I just checked the red lights, but emotionally... emotionally I just feel like this horrible person. I sit there staring at the screens, and part of me really, truly believes that if anything goes wrong on my watch—if a dealer gets assaulted, if a huge scam goes through, if anyone gets hurt—that I deserve to be punished for it. I feel like I'm just waiting for the hammer to fall, because I'm so incompetent that I'm putting everyone in the casino at risk. It's this deep, sinking feeling that I have no value, that I'm just a liability taking up space in that room. It's not just fear, it's... it's knowing, deep down, that I'm exactly as bad as those voices say I am.
Do you feel any physical sensations, such as numbness, tingling, or pain, when you hear the voices through the monitor speakers?

Well, numbness or tingling? No... no, not really. And not pain either. I mean, I don't feel any actual physical pain when it happens. It's not like a sharp pain or pins and needles or anything like that. It's more just... well, like I was trying to explain earlier, it's that intense rush of ice water in my veins. That cold, sinking drop in my stomach. But I wouldn't call that numbness, you know? If anything, I feel entirely too aware of everything. 

When I'm sitting there in that surveillance room, and the air conditioning is blowing, and then suddenly I hear them coming through the speakers, telling me that I missed it, that I'm messing up... I don't go numb at all. My hands shake, yes, when I'm reaching out to check the red mute lights on the console, but that's just from the sheer terror of it all. It's not a tingling kind of shaking. And I'll be sweating, just sitting there in the dim light, hoping Marcus doesn't walk back in and see me falling apart. 

But actual physical pain from the voices? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the crushing weight of it. That heavy, wet wool blanket feeling I mentioned, where I just feel so exhausted and weighed down by the guilt and the dread. I feel it in my body, sure, like a terrible heaviness, but it's not a pain or a tingling. It's just... it's just the physical toll of being so incredibly scared and feeling so completely worthless while I'm trapped in that room staring at those screens, waiting for the shift to end. So, no, nothing like numbness or pain. Just the shaking and the heaviness.
Have you ever experienced anything like this before in your life, where you heard voices or had similar feelings of dread and guilt?

No, doctor, never. Honestly, that's part of why it's so terrifying to me. I've been doing this kind of work for a long time, and before this current stretch... this whole period where I've just been feeling so incredibly hopeless and overwhelmed by guilt... I had never experienced anything even remotely like this. 

It really all seemed to start after the surveillance lead change at work. When management shifted around, things just started feeling so heavy, and I started sinking into this really low period. But before that? Never. I had never sat at a console and heard accusations coming through the equipment. I've spent years staring at those exact same monitors, listening to the exact same hum of the AC, and the speakers were always just regular speakers. They never spoke to me, they never told me I was missing things, and I certainly never felt this absolute, terrifying certainty that I was dangerous to everyone on the casino floor. 

I keep trying to think back, you know? When I'm sitting there in the dark and the voices start up, I try to rack my brain, trying to remember if I ever felt this way in my twenties or thirties, or back when I first got my degree and started out. But I didn't. I used to be so confident in my catches. I was good at my job. It's like the voices, and that crushing dread, and these awful beliefs that I'm responsible for terrible things... they only seem to be part of this one, specific low period I'm in right now. It all just arrived together after that lead change, like this massive dark cloud that just won't lift. So, no, nothing like this before in my entire life. Just now. Just this one, awful stretch.
Have you ever had a period in your life where you felt similarly overwhelmed by guilt and dread, even if the voices weren't present?

Well, no... not really. I mean, I've had times where I felt bad about a mistake, sure. Everyone does, right? Like, years ago, back when I was first starting out in surveillance, I missed a pretty obvious chip-capping trick at a blackjack table. I felt terrible about it for a few days, kicking myself, replaying the tape in my head. But that was just normal regret. It wasn't this... this all-consuming, heavy dread that I feel now. 

I've never had a time where the guilt felt like a physical weight, where it just completely took over my life. Before this current stretch, before everything shifted at work with the new lead, I was actually a pretty level-headed person. I could leave work at work. If I made a bad call or missed something minor, I'd learn from it and move on. I never sat in the dark, sweating, convinced that I was a fundamental danger to the people around me. 

So, no, even without the voices, I've never experienced anything close to this level of guilt and dread. It's like this entirely new, horrible thing that just swallowed me up all at once. I keep trying to understand why it's so different now, why it feels so much bigger and more real than any normal mistake I've ever made. It's just... it's just so heavy, doctor. It's like I'm carrying the weight of every potential disaster in that casino on my shoulders, and I've never felt anything like that before in my entire life. Not until this dark cloud rolled in.
Have you ever lost touch with reality for a period of time while experiencing these voices?

Lost touch with reality? I... well, I don't think so. I mean, what does that really mean, anyway? Because when I'm sitting there in the surveillance room, staring at the bank of monitors—usually the ones covering the high-limit baccarat tables, because that's where the most action is, and where the most risk is—and the voices start coming through the speakers... it feels completely real. It feels like the most real thing in the world. 

But if you mean, do I black out? Or do I wake up somewhere and not know how I got there, or forget who I am? No, nothing like that. I know exactly where I am. I'm in chair number three, in the dark, with the AC humming, and my hands shaking, and Marcus usually sitting two stations down, completely oblivious. I know I'm at work. I know I'm supposed to be watching for card counters or bet capping. I never forget that. 

It's just that... the voices are happening *while* I'm doing all that. They're telling me I missed a drop, or that I'm letting someone walk out with thousands, and that it's going to ruin everything. And I'm sitting there, trying to watch the screens, trying to do my job, but I'm also listening to them, because they sound just like the pit bosses calling up, only... meaner. So much meaner. And they know everything I'm doing wrong. 

So, no, I don't lose touch with where I am or what I'm doing. I'm painfully aware of every second that ticks by on the digital clock above the monitors. I remember everything that happens. I remember the sweat on my palms, I remember the exact shade of green on the felt of the tables on screen four... I just also hear them. And I feel that awful, crushing weight. But I'm still there, in the room, the whole time. I never float away or lose time or anything like that. I'm just trapped right there in it.
Have you ever had any other experiences where you heard or saw things that others couldn't?

Well, seeing things, no. I've never seen anything that wasn't there. My eyes are glued to those monitors for ten hours a day, and I see exactly what the cameras see. But hearing things... yes. That's... well, honestly, doctor, that's the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in. It's what scared me enough to realize I needed help. 

Because, like I said, I sit in that surveillance room, right? And we have these quiet stretches. Sometimes it's 3:00 AM on a Tuesday, and the floor is practically dead. Just a few stragglers at the penny slots and maybe one sleepy dealer at a $10 blackjack table. It gets so quiet in our room that you can hear the hum of the servers down the hall. And I'll be sitting there, and I'll have my monitor channels completely muted. Every single one. I double-check the little red light on the console to make sure. But then... then I'll hear them. 

The voices come right through the monitor speakers. It's not a whisper in my ear, it's not a thought in my head. It's electronic, coming through the equipment. And they'll say my name. They'll say, "You missed it, Ruth." Or they'll say, "People are going to get hurt because of you." And it's so clear. It's as clear as if the pit boss was calling up on the secure line. But the phone isn't ringing. And the channels are muted. 

I even asked Marcus once. He was sitting two stations down, eating a sandwich, totally relaxed. I leaned over and asked, "Did you hear dispatch say something just now?" And he just looked at me like I was crazy and said, "Ruth, the radio's been dead for an hour." He didn't hear a thing. No one else hears anything. Just me. And it just keeps happening during those quiet stretches, telling me I'm failing, telling me I'm putting people in danger. It's terrifying, doctor. It's absolutely terrifying to hear something so clearly when you know the volume is at zero.
Was there something specific happening in your life or at work around the time you first started hearing the voices?

Well, yes, actually, there was. I think I touched on it a little bit earlier, but it really all goes back to when they brought in the new surveillance lead at the casino. Before that happened, before this whole awful stretch of just feeling completely hopeless and weighed down by this unbearable guilt, things were fine. I mean, I was fine. We had this restructuring, and the new lead came in, and the entire atmosphere in the monitoring room just shifted. It became so intense, so hyper-critical, and I just started feeling so incredibly down and overwhelmed by it all. I would drive home after a shift and just sit in my car in the driveway for an hour because I felt too heavy, too exhausted and guilty to even walk up to my own front door. 

And it was only after that heavy feeling really set in... after I was already deep in this awful, low period, that the voices actually started. Before this stretch, I had never, ever heard accusations coming through the muted equipment. Never in my life. And I certainly never felt so absolutely certain that I was a danger to everyone around me. It is like the voices and those terrifying beliefs only seem to be a part of this same low period. They didn't just happen out of nowhere on their own. 

The hopelessness and the guilt started right after that lead change, and then it just spiraled, and suddenly the monitors are accusing me of ruining lives and missing drops. It all just belongs to this one long, dark stretch I am in right now. I mean, I have been doing this job for years, watching screens, logging incidents, dealing with the stress of the floor, and I have never experienced anything even remotely like this until that management shift triggered all this hopelessness. It just feels like my mind couldn't take the weight of feeling like a failure, and now I am stuck with these voices on top of it.
Have you ever felt like the voices were a part of your own thoughts, or did they always seem to be coming from outside of you?

Like I was saying a minute ago, they definitely aren't my own thoughts. I mean, I know what my own thoughts sound like, you know? If I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, I need to pick up milk on the way home," or "I wonder if Marcus is going to take his break soon," that's inside my head. I feel that happening behind my eyes. But these voices... no, they are entirely outside of me. 

Like I mentioned before, that specific thing is exactly what scared me enough to finally come in and see you. Because during those quiet stretches in the surveillance room, the sound is physically coming right through the monitor speakers. It's not an internal monologue at all. It has that tinny, slight electronic distortion that our console speakers have. When they say, "You missed it, Ruth," or when they tell me, "People are going to get hurt because of you," it has actual volume in the room. It has direction. I can physically turn my head toward the sound, like I'll look right at the little black speaker mounted under monitor four, and the sound feels like it's vibrating right out of that specific piece of plastic and metal. 

And that's why it's so incredibly terrifying, doctor. Because I *know* every channel is muted. I press the master mute, I see the little red indicator light shining right at me, but the sound still pushes through the air from the outside. If it was just a thought, I never would have leaned over and asked Marcus if he heard dispatch that one time, right? Because you don't ask someone if they heard your own thoughts. You ask if they heard a noise in the room. And to me, it is a noise in the room. It's an external, physical noise coming from the equipment, hitting my eardrums from the outside, even when I know the volume is off and no one else in the room hears a single thing.
Have you ever had any other episodes in your life where you heard voices or saw things that weren't there, outside of the surveillance room?

Outside of work? No... no, never. It's... like I was saying, doctor, I know I keep coming back to this same point, but it really is just completely confined to that one specific place. Just the surveillance room. I've never been at home, you know, making dinner or walking through the grocery store and heard anything out of the ordinary. Never. It's only ever when I'm sitting in that chair, staring at those screens. 

And I think... well, I think that's why it took me a little while to realize how bad things had gotten, because I could leave work and the voices wouldn't follow me to my house. But even so, it's... I mean, I know I keep repeating myself, but it's what scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and come in to see you. Because it's just so incredibly real when I'm there. 

It always happens during those really long, quiet stretches in the room, when the casino floor is dead and I'm just sitting there with the hum of the air conditioner and the servers. That's exactly when the voices come right through those monitor speakers. Just drilling into me, saying, "You missed it, Ruth," or... or "People are going to get hurt because of you." And I know I already explained about the mute button earlier, but I just can't emphasize enough how absolutely terrifying it is to sit there, staring at a console where every single channel is completely muted—the red indicator lights are glowing right at me, the volume sliders are pulled all the way down to zero—and I still hear those accusations so clearly. And then I look around, and Marcus or whoever else is on shift is just sipping their coffee, totally oblivious, because no one else hears anything at all. It’s just me, and it’s just in that room, but it’s enough to make me feel like I'm completely losing my grip.
Do you hear the voices every time you are in the surveillance room or are there times when you don't hear them at all?

Well, it's not every single second I'm in there, thank goodness, or I think I really would have just walked out and never come back. It's... well, like I was mentioning just a few minutes ago, and I know I keep circling back to this exact same thing, but it really is the whole reason I got so terrified that I finally made this appointment. It happens specifically during those quiet stretches. 

You see, a casino shift has a rhythm to it. If it's a Friday night and the floor is packed, we are tracking a dozen different tables, dealing with pit bosses, logging incidents... it's busy. There's actual noise and activity. And during those busy times, I don't hear them at all. I'm just doing my job, feeling awful and heavy with that guilt I talked about, sure, but no voices. 

But it's the lulls. The dead times. Like a Tuesday at 4 AM when nothing is happening on the floor. That is when it happens. When it gets completely quiet. Like I told you before, I'll be sitting there, I know for an absolute fact the channels are completely muted, I've checked the red indicator lights a hundred times... and right through those monitor speakers, that's when they start up. Saying, you know, you missed it, Ruth, or telling me that people are going to get hurt because of me. 

And it's just so incredibly isolating, because Marcus is sitting right there, and it's so quiet you could hear a pin drop in that room, and he hears absolutely nothing. Not a peep. But for me, the speakers are just broadcasting these awful, terrifying things. So, no, it's not every single time I walk in the door, but it's every time the room gets quiet... and that's what scared me enough to come in, because I just sit there absolutely dreading the quiet parts of my shift now, just waiting for the equipment to start talking to me again.
Do you hear the voices every single day when you're at work, or are there days when they don't happen at all?

Well, it really depends on the rotation they have me on for that week, you know? Because my schedule fluctuates. So, no, it's not every single day, but that's only because not every day has those lulls. If I get put on a heavy weekend shift—like a Friday or a Saturday where there's a big poker tournament or just wall-to-wall bachelor parties—I might actually go the entire twelve hours without it happening once. Because on those days, we're constantly talking, constantly switching cameras, calling down to the floor... there's just no downtime. 

But on the days where I'm working a Tuesday mid-morning or a Wednesday overnight... yes. Every single one of those days. And I know I am sounding like an absolute broken record here, doctor, I really do know I keep bringing us right back to this exact same scenario, but you have to understand that this specific experience is the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. It's what scared me enough to finally come in. 

Because on those slower days, the minute the floor empties out and we hit one of those quiet stretches in the surveillance room, I just know it's coming. I'll literally sit there staring at the console, double-checking that every single channel is muted, praying that it won't happen this time. But it always does. The audio feeds will be completely dead, but those voices will just push right through the monitor speakers anyway, telling me, "You missed it, Ruth," or warning me that people are going to get hurt because of me. And it happens day after day after day, as long as the room gets quiet. I'll just be gripping the edge of the desk, listening to these horrible things coming out of the equipment, and whoever is working the desk next to me won't even flinch because no one else hears anything. So, if it's a busy day, I'm safe. But if it's a slow day... I hear them every single time.
Do you think the voices are something that is happening inside your head or are they definitely coming from the monitor speakers?

That is... well, that is exactly the question I keep asking myself, doctor. And I know, I know I am just beating a dead horse here because I keep bringing up the exact same details over and over, but I really need you to understand why this has me so completely rattled. 

To me, in that moment? They are absolutely, one hundred percent coming out of those physical speakers. It doesn't sound like a thought. You know what your own thoughts sound like, they're inside your skull, they have a certain internal feeling. This is completely external. I can hear the slight static, the tinny, compressed quality of the audio equipment we use. We have these black, rectangular monitors mounted right at ear level across the console, and when it happens—during those awful quiet stretches I keep telling you about—the sound physically hits my ears from the outside. It's a broadcast. 

And I know I've said this a dozen times already today, but that is exactly the thing that terrified me so much that I finally picked up the phone to make this appointment. Because my logical brain is telling me, Ruth, you are looking right at the mute button. The channels are completely dead. Whoever is sitting next to you isn't reacting to anything at all. But my ears are hearing, clear as day, pushing right through the mesh of those monitors, those exact words... telling me I missed it, telling me people are going to get hurt because of me.

The hopelessness and the guilt started right after that lead change, and then it just spiraled, and suddenly the monitors are accusing me of ruining lives and missing drops. It all just belongs to this one long, dark stretch I am in right now. I mean, I have been doing this job for years, watching screens, logging incidents, dealing with the stress of the floor, and I have never experienced anything even remotely like this until that management shift triggered all this hopelessness. It just feels like my mind couldn't take the weight of feeling like a failure, and now I am stuck with these voices on top of it.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt like the voices were a part of your own thoughts, or did they always seem to be coming from outside of you?

patient.answer:
Like I was saying a minute ago, they definitely aren't my own thoughts. I mean, I know what my own thoughts sound like, you know? If I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, I need to pick up milk on the way home," or "I wonder if Marcus is going to take his break soon," that's inside my head. I feel that happening behind my eyes. But these voices... no, they are entirely outside of me. 

Like I mentioned before, that specific thing is exactly what scared me enough to finally come in and see you. Because during those quiet stretches in the surveillance room, the sound is physically coming right through the monitor speakers. It's not an internal monologue at all. It has that tinny, slight electronic distortion that our console speakers have. When they say, "You missed it, Ruth," or when they tell me, "People are going to get hurt because of you," it has actual volume in the room. It has direction. I can physically turn my head toward the sound, like I'll look right at the little black speaker mounted under monitor four, and the sound feels like it's vibrating right out of that specific piece of plastic and metal. 

And that's why it's so incredibly terrifying, doctor. Because I *know* every channel is muted. I press the master mute, I see the little red indicator light shining right at me, but the sound still pushes through the air from the outside. If it was just a thought, I never would have leaned over and asked Marcus if he heard dispatch that one time, right? Because you don't ask someone if they heard your own thoughts. You ask if they heard a noise in the room. And to me, it is a noise in the room. It's an external, physical noise coming from the equipment, hitting my eardrums from the outside, even when I know the volume is off and no one else in the room hears a single thing.

patient.answer:
Outside of work? No... no, never. It's... like I was saying, doctor, I know I keep coming back to this same point, but it really is just completely confined to that one specific place. Just the surveillance room. I've never been at home, you know, making dinner or walking through the grocery store and heard anything out of the ordinary. Never. It's only ever when I'm sitting in that chair, staring at those screens. 

And I think... well, I think that's why it took me a little while to realize how bad things had gotten, because I could leave work and the voices wouldn't follow me to my house. But even so, it's... I mean, I know I keep repeating myself, but it's what scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and come in to see you. Because it's just so incredibly real when I'm there. 

It always happens during those really long, quiet stretches in the room, when the casino floor is dead and I'm just sitting there with the hum of the air conditioner and the servers. That's exactly when the voices come right through those monitor speakers. Just drilling into me, saying, "You missed it, Ruth," or... or "People are going to get hurt because of you." And I know I already explained about the mute button earlier, but I just can't emphasize enough how absolutely terrifying it is to sit there, staring at a console where every single channel is completely muted—the red indicator lights are glowing right at me, the volume sliders are pulled all the way down to zero—and I still hear those accusations so clearly. And then I look around, and Marcus or whoever else is on shift is just sipping their coffee, totally oblivious, because no one else hears anything at all. It’s just me, and it’s just in that room, but it’s enough to make me feel like I'm completely losing my grip.

doctor.question: Do you hear the voices every time you are in the surveillance room or are there times when you don't hear them at all?

patient.answer:
Well, it's not every single second I'm in there, thank goodness, or I think I really would have just walked out and never come back. It's... well, like I was mentioning just a few minutes ago, and I know I keep circling back to this exact same thing, but it really is the whole reason I got so terrified that I finally made this appointment. It happens specifically during those quiet stretches. 

You see, a casino shift has a rhythm to it. If it's a Friday night and the floor is packed, we are tracking a dozen different tables, dealing with pit bosses, logging incidents... it's busy. There's actual noise and activity. And during those busy times, I don't hear them at all. I'm just doing my job, feeling awful and heavy with that guilt I talked about, sure, but no voices. 

But it's the lulls. The dead times. Like a Tuesday at 4 AM when nothing is happening on the floor. That is when it happens. When it gets completely quiet. Like I told you before, I'll be sitting there, I know for an absolute fact the channels are completely muted, I've checked the red indicator lights a hundred times... and right through those monitor speakers, that's when they start up. Saying, you know, you missed it, Ruth, or telling me that people are going to get hurt because of me. 

And it's just so incredibly isolating, because Marcus is sitting right there, and it's so quiet you could hear a pin drop in that room, and he hears absolutely nothing. Not a peep. But for me, the speakers are just broadcasting these awful, terrifying things. So, no, it's not every single time I walk in the door, but it's every time the room gets quiet... and that's what scared me enough to come in, because I just sit there absolutely dreading the quiet parts of my shift now, just waiting for the equipment to start talking to me again.

doctor.question: Do you hear the voices every single day when you're at work, or are there days when they don't happen at all?

patient.answer:
Well, it really depends on the rotation they have me on for that week, you know? Because my schedule fluctuates. So, no, it's not every single day, but that's only because not every day has those lulls. If I get put on a heavy weekend shift—like a Friday or a Saturday where there's a big poker tournament or just wall-to-wall bachelor parties—I might actually go the entire twelve hours without it happening once. Because on those days, we're constantly talking, constantly switching cameras, calling down to the floor... there's just no downtime. 

But on the days where I'm working a Tuesday mid-morning or a Wednesday overnight... yes. Every single one of those days. And I know I am sounding like an absolute broken record here, doctor, I really do know I keep bringing us right back to this exact same scenario, but you have to understand that this specific experience is the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. It's what scared me enough to finally come in. 

Because on those slower days, the minute the floor empties out and we hit one of those quiet stretches in the surveillance room, I just know it's coming. I'll literally sit there staring at the console, double-checking that every single channel is muted, praying that it won't happen this time. But it always does. The audio feeds will be completely dead, but those voices will just push right through the monitor speakers anyway, telling me, "You missed it, Ruth," or warning me that people are going to get hurt because of me. And it happens day after day after day, as long as the room gets quiet. I'll just be gripping the edge of the desk, listening to these horrible things coming out of the equipment, and whoever is working the desk next to me won't even flinch because no one else hears anything. So, if it's a busy day, I'm safe. But if it's a slow day... I hear them every single time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the voices are a result of an external stimulus or internal thoughts
doctor.question: Do you think the voices are something that is happening inside your head or are they definitely coming from the monitor speakers?

target_item.name: Hallucinations

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the origin and perception of the voices, which directly relates to my hallucinations.

patient.answer:
That is... well, that is exactly the question I keep asking myself, doctor. And I know, I know I am just beating a dead horse here because I keep bringing up the exact same details over and over, but I really need you to understand why this has me so completely rattled. 

To me, in that moment? They are absolutely, one hundred percent coming out of those physical speakers. It doesn't sound like a thought. You know what your own thoughts sound like, they're inside your skull, they have a certain internal feeling. This is completely external. I can hear the slight static, the tinny, compressed quality of the audio equipment we use. We have these black, rectangular monitors mounted right at ear level across the console, and when it happens—during those awful quiet stretches I keep telling you about—the sound physically hits my ears from the outside. It's a broadcast. 

And I know I've said this a dozen times already today, but that is exactly the thing that terrified me so much that I finally picked up the phone to make this appointment. Because my logical brain is telling me, Ruth, you are looking right at the mute button. The channels are completely dead. Whoever is sitting next to you isn't reacting to anything at all. But my ears are hearing, clear as day, pushing right through the mesh of those monitors, those exact words... telling me I missed it, telling me people are going to get hurt because of me. 

I've even leaned in close to the equipment when it happens, literally putting my ear right up against the plastic casing, trying to see if there's a short circuit, or some kind of weird radio frequency interference from a walkie-talkie down on the casino floor, because it sounds that real. It doesn't feel like it's in my head. It feels like the machinery itself is speaking to me, judging me. If it just felt like my own imagination acting up, maybe I wouldn't be sitting here in your office. But the fact that I cannot distinguish between a real security feed and those accusations coming through the muted speakers... that is what I just can't handle anymore.
